headline: Claude Walker initiates small research position in Sonic Healthcare, attracted by defensive pathology networks and historically high dividend yield of ~5%
reasoning: Walker sees Sonic Healthcare's global pathology distribution and testing networks as stable, defensive assets. While capital-intensive with thin margins, the low returns on capital in the industry deter new competitors, keeping the competitive environment relatively stable. The stock is trading at a historically elevated dividend yield of approximately 4.9–5% partially franked, which Walker views as a better-than-bank-account return. Even modest capital growth over the long term could make this an attractive total return proposition given the yield.
quote: Sonic Healthcare is the first one. This is probably your your more blue chip option. It is. The majority of its revenue comes from pathology. Uh, distribution and testing networks all around the world. Has Europe, uh, you know, Australia, US. It also has a radiology business. But the assets that I'm interested in are the pathology distribution networks, because I basically believe that although distribution networks are not the best quality business because their capital intensive to build plus then have small margins... they are kind of stable businesses because those lowest returns on capital discourage new competitors. So often the sort of competitive situation is just stable and not too difficult. So I like it for its defensive features. Sonic. And on top of that, it's trading at, you know, a historically high dividend yield at the moment... it's still at quite a high level for that 5% partially franked or 4.9% partially franked. Uh, so that's a fairly good return. Like, you know, better than a bank account.

So his family, he and his family, they own over 50% of the business. So honestly, it's kind of their way of the highway kind of situation... it's like an office releasing kind of, um, business where essentially they hire, you know, a whole floor and then rent it out to like smaller groups of people and, you know, provide tech infrastructure around that as well. So essentially, what you're in it for is the dividend. And and they are they have a reason to want to pay dividends. Right. Because they're paying it to themselves.

headline: CGT changes expected to dampen demand for ASX growth stocks and shift capital to income-producing dividend plays
reasoning: Claude Walker argues that recent changes to Australian tax laws make it less attractive to hold growth assets in personal names, as investors may face a large tax bill in one bumpy year even if they lose money in other years. This creates a degree of paralysis around buying growth stocks for some period — potentially a year or more. Capital is flowing toward income-producing stocks in the short term as a result. Walker notes this doesn't mean he has abandoned growth investing, but for money held in his personal name, dividend stocks are more attractive right now, with growth assets better suited to superannuation or structures that allow profit smoothing.
quote: I think what we've seen is the changes to the tax laws mean that it doesn't make sense to invest in growth assets in your own personal, uh, capacity anymore. It makes more sense to invest, uh, in growth assets, for example, in your superannuation or in some other structure that allows you to smooth out the profits over multiple years rather than have otherwise. You might have just one bulky year where you pay top tax rate even though you lose money in the other years. So are essentially think that that's going to put a little bit of paralysis around buying a lot of growth stocks, uh, for some amount of time, maybe a year or more. I don't really know how long it takes this kind of thing to work through the system, but and we've seen basically where that capital is going is more in the short term to income producing stocks.

headline: Claude Walker rates EOS a sell on valuation but concedes momentum traders may want to hold given strong defense thematic
reasoning: Walker agrees with the defense thematic and notes Australia has very few genuine listed defense companies, with drone warfare a new reality creating strong demand for cheap counter-drone systems. However, as a fundamental investor requiring free cash flow backed valuations, he finds EOS too hard to predict and already too highly valued. He suggests taking profits on valuation grounds but acknowledges that with a strong thematic, holding some exposure while letting momentum run is a reasonable approach for momentum-oriented investors.
quote: As a fundamental investor myself, someone who really does want to have a valuation backed by my estimates of future free cash flow. This one's too hard to predict for me and the valuation is just too high already. So for me, it would be, I guess, a sell essentially. But that's on valuation. And I don't think that people should always sell on valuation. I think that it makes sense when you've got a hot stock that's a great thematic. Yeah, sell a little on valuation, but let it let it run a little bit to is my general rule, even when it's overvalued. So, yeah, OK, take profits at the moment. But just because the thematic is so good, I don't see any valuation support on it right now, though.

headline: Claude Walker reiterates strong buy on Energy One, comparing its setup to early-stage ProMedicus and flagging Wilson Asset Management re-entry
reasoning: Walker has been a long-term bull on Energy One and notes the company updated under its new CEO with ARR growth of 13% versus prior guidance of 15-20%, citing delayed contracts. He argues this is one of the most common and believable reasons to miss on ARR. Wilson Asset Management has been buying again after previously trading it well (buying at ~$11, selling at $18-20). Walker considers Energy One the closest thing he can find to early ProMedicus — a profitable, growing, sticky SaaS business with strong tailwinds — and rates it a strong buy.
quote: We got an update from the company, the first one under the new CEO, a really lengthy missive from him that is great to see how he's thinking about it and taking ownership of the future. However, the bad news was the AR growth is going to be 13 percent and the market was expecting the company was expecting 15 to 20 percent. Now, the reason for the slight growth was they say just delayed contracts into the next year, which is totally believable. It's one of the most common reasons that people miss on ARR. And the final tidbit is that I think Wilson Asset Management have been buying again and they traded it perfectly last time. They bought it around 11 or something and then they sold a bunch of like 18 to 20 and now they're back buying again. So, look, if you don't trust me, trust those. Well, trust them on that particular stock because they've got a great track record of calling it.

headline: Claude Walker discusses 'SaaSapocalypse' sentiment creating broad indiscriminate selling in SaaS stocks, creating selective buying opportunities in quality operators
reasoning: Claude identified a theme of irrational, sentiment-driven selling affecting all SaaS stocks regardless of individual quality, driven by fears around AI displacement of software businesses and broader market pessimism. He believes this is creating significant mispricings in profitable, growing SaaS companies like Kinatico and Energy One that do not face existential AI risk. He views compliance-driven software as particularly resilient because customers need accountability, not just functionality.
quote: A big part of the share price decline you've seen since December last year has to do with the fact that there was this Saspocalypse kind of thing. People got very scared that software companies, you know, are basically doomed. And I don't take that view personally. I do think that, yeah, some will be impacted, some perhaps impacted badly. Maybe Kinatico will be impacted, but at the same time, this is a compliance kind of software. And a lot of the reason actually for a lot of software, it's not people don't just want something that does the job. They want someone to blame.

headline: Claude Walker warns new Australian CGT rules have created a buyer strike in personally-held small-cap and biotech stocks, distorting prices ahead of June 30
reasoning: Claude argued that the change to CGT rules has made investing in high-risk/reward stocks under a personal name tax-inefficient, as winners would be taxed at up to 47% compared to 30% for companies. This has caused a wave of tax-loss selling in small and microcap stocks and simultaneously dried up buyers. He noted this snowballs: falling prices create more loss-selling, compressing valuations well below fundamental value. He expected a recovery in affected names post-June 30 once the artificial selling pressure abates.
quote: These are the exact kind of stocks that have basically had a complete drought of buyers now because of the new CGT rules. If someone was investing in their own personal name in biotech stocks, it just stops making sense to do it now... there's just been in these kind of high risk rolled small caps. There's an absolute strike of buyers because nobody who is buying in their personal name wants to buy anymore. And the people that want to keep doing it, they've got to go and, you know, set up a different structure and stuff like that if they want it to be tax optimized.

They're not controlling their demand. You know, insurance customers are huge, bigger than them, people who can like have a lot of power over them and negotiate really hard margins. Just a bad business.

headline: Claude Walker bullish on ASX defense thematic as drone warfare creates strong demand, with very few genuine listed defense plays available
reasoning: Walker notes Australia has very few genuine listed defense companies on the ASX, making those that are listed beneficiaries of strong thematic momentum. headline: Claude Walker rates Control Bionics a sell citing negligible revenue growth and no near-term path to profitability
reasoning: Walker notes that despite genuinely cool technology enabling communication for non-verbal people and expansion into sports monitoring and rehab, revenue has grown from $4m in FY2021 to only $6.1m in FY2025 — very slow for a still-loss-making business. The company is dependent on government and NDIS approvals which slow commercialization. Walker says he liked the company at listing in 2021 but the lack of revenue growth means it won't reach profitability soon and he rates it a sell until it gets much closer to profitability.
quote: I don't think that it's going to make a profit soon. And the reason for that is that the today, since listing the historical revenue growth has been extremely low. So that, you know, in 2021, FY 2021, they had like four million revenue, which is very small. And then that would have been OK if it was growing, you know, at 30 percent a year. But fast forward four years and we're and in FY 2025, they only did six point one million revenue. So that to me says that the growth is very slow. And whilst they are still making, you know, losses worth a significant percentage of their revenue, I think it's safe to say they're not going to be profitable anytime soon.

headline: Claude Walker holds Wagner Holdings for now but looks to trim, flagging unusually high earnings growth expectations for a capital-intensive business that imply record margins

headline: Claude Walker holds GWA Group at a low multiple with modest upside from government housing stimulus, but warns on inflation risk and recession sensitivity
reasoning: GWA is not a high-quality business but trades at a low multiple that reflects this. Government housing policy could provide a moderate tailwind for bathroom and kitchen fittings demand over coming years. However, the inflationary environment increases working capital requirements, and a recession would hit demand sharply. Claude calls it a hold for those already in it but not an exciting entry point.
quote: Right now, if we look at it, the multiple's quite low, and the budget changes really does seem like very geared towards like new housing construction. So I wouldn't be surprised if conditions over the next few years did ease for these guys.

headline: Claude Walker calls WT Financial a buy at ~6% dividend yield but recommends splitting exposure with Centrepoint to dilute licensee blow-up risk
reasoning: WT Financial and Centrepoint Alliance are both cheap roll-ups of financial advisor licensees trading at modest multiples with good dividend yields. headline: Claude Walker buys Energy One weakness after 13% ARR guidance miss, arguing the delay reflects expanding customer project scopes rather than demand deterioration
reasoning: EOL guided to ~13% ARR growth in FY26 versus a 15-20% target, primarily due to timing delays on two large multinational industrial customers who expanded their project scopes. Claude views this as essentially neutral to slightly positive long-term — the delayed revenue flows into FY27 and the scope expansions signal strong customer engagement. headline: Avoided as a messy, cyclical advertising business with volatile historical earnings and limited enduring value
reasoning: SEG is fundamentally an advertising business, making it pro-cyclical with erratic historical earnings driven by asset acquisitions, divestitures, and write-downs. Claude sees no clear path to building enduring value and thinks the cheapness argument ('it's priced in') rarely holds for these types of companies. He acknowledges share buybacks but remains unconvinced.
quote: This is a real mess. It's a real tough business, basically. Hard to make money, hard to build enduring value. So I would just avoid it, like quite frankly.

headline: Claude Walker argues proposed CGT indexing changes are disproportionately punitive for growth stock investors relative to index fund or property investors
reasoning: Claude explains that the budget's proposed CGT cost-base indexing only applies to the winning stock, not the portfolio's losers, meaning a growth investor who makes the same nominal profit as an ETF investor over 10 years will pay materially more tax. This structural disadvantage should reduce the relative valuation of growth stocks across the board, as the pre-tax return required to match an index fund increases. He describes it as specifically detrimental to his style of small-cap growth investing.
quote: For the small cap growth investor...you might have a number of stocks that lose out completely, but just one stock that accounts for the vast majority of returns...you'll end up paying like the full, probably marginal rate...And that will encourage people not to be growth investors and instead to just invest safely in like indexes or ironically even houses.
